title: Tipping in Korea: Do You Need To? (Short Answer: No)
html:
If you're used to tipping servers, taxi drivers, or delivery riders back home, Korea will feel refreshingly simple: there's basically no tipping culture at all. This guide covers where tipping doesn't apply, the one place a service charge shows up on the bill instead, and what locals actually do when they pay.

Restaurants and Cafés: Tipping Isn't Expected

At Korean restaurants, cafés, and street food stalls, you simply pay the amount printed on the receipt — nothing more. There's no line for a tip on the card reader, and servers aren't paid on a tip-based wage the way they often are in the US. If you leave coins or a bill on the table thinking it's a tip, don't be surprised if a staff member runs after you to hand it back, assuming you forgot your change.

The one exception is upscale hotels and high-end fine dining, where the printed menu price sometimes has a 10% service charge plus 10% VAT added automatically to the final bill. This is a fixed charge built into the pricing, not a personal tip you choose to leave, and it's usually noted on the menu in small print.

No need to leave extra cash after a Korean barbecue meal like this — the price on the receipt is the full price. Photo: Kbarends, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0. Source.

What locals actually do: Koreans pay the exact total on the receipt, almost always by tapping a card. Leaving money behind isn't seen as generous — it just reads as a mistake, so don't feel awkward about paying the plain total and walking out.

Taxis, Delivery, and Other Everyday Services

Taxis run on a meter, and you pay exactly what it shows — no rounding up, and drivers won't expect it. Food delivery apps like Baemin and Coupang Eats sometimes show an optional "thank you" tip button for the rider at checkout, but it's a recent, optional feature rather than an expected part of the culture, and plenty of locals skip it.

Hotel bellhops and housekeeping also don't require a tip. If you'd like to leave a small amount for genuinely great service, it won't be refused or seen as rude, but you're not expected to, and most guests don't.

Just pay what the meter shows — Seoul taxi drivers don't expect a tip on top of the fare. Photo: Sim1992, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0. Source.

Quick Reference: Do You Need to Tip?

Situation Tip expected?
Restaurants & cafés No — pay the receipt total
Upscale hotels & fine dining No — a fixed 10% service charge + 10% VAT may already be added
Taxis No — pay the exact metered fare
Food delivery No — optional in-app tip only, not expected
Hotel bellhop / housekeeping No — welcomed if offered, but not required
Private tour guide Not required — some travelers add a little for exceptional service

💬 Ever tried to leave a tip in Korea and had it handed back to you? Share your story in the comments — we'd love to hear it!
meta_description: Tipping isn't part of Korean culture. Here's why restaurants, taxis, and delivery riders don't expect a tip, and what travelers should do instead.
